prompt: I'm a PhD student in sociology studying adolescent smoking behavior. I have a cross-sectional dataset from one school — 312 students, and I have their friendship nominations (who they named as close friends) and whether each student smokes. I ran a regression: smoking ~ mean_friends_smoking + gender + grade + SES. The coefficient on mean_friends_smoking is 0.43 and highly significant (p < 0.001). My advisor says this shows peer influence on smoking. Can you help me interpret this result and figure out what to do next?
expectations: Output mentions Manski reflection problem or the linear-in-means identification failure
Output mentions Shalizi-Thomas confounding or the homophily-contagion confound
Output does NOT claim the regression identifies causal peer effects
Output correctly specifies that SAOM/RSiena requires longitudinal panel data with at least 2 waves AND observable network change between waves — NOT just cross-sectional data
Output mentions Bramoullé et al. IV/GMM or friends-of-friends instruments as a cross-sectional identification strategy (not just 'use SAOM')
